newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - BTR plans selling another 25 firms.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - BTR plans selling another 25 firms.

text.p: Industrial conglomerate BTR Plc, which earlier reported a 13.4 percent fall in 1996 profits, said it planned to sell about two dozen mostly smaller units to complete its divestment drive by the end of the year.

"They are relatively small sized (as) the big ones have gone but there is still somewhere in the order of 25 companies to be sold in the balance of the year," chief executive Ian Strachan told journalists on Thursday.
With over 1,000 subsidiaries across the globe, BTR wants to focus on its manufacturing and engineering operations and divest other, non-core assets to improve its performance.

Pre-tax profit fell to 1.301 billion stg from 1.503 billion in 1995. "The results confirm that we are delivering against our strategy that we announced last year," said Strachan, after BTR earlier said it expected steady underlying growth this year.
The pound's current strength would fail to have a significant impact, as most of the group's transactions are handled in many other currencies than sterling, Strachan said.
Last year's group result would have been hit by 50 million stg if the pound had been trading at current levels for the whole year.
This impact would result from "translating" profits posted abroad into pounds, Strachan said.
He forecast profits in BTR's automotive sector to pick up in 1997 after they fell 11 percent last year amid difficult trading conditions in Europe and South America.
But 1997's automotive result should improve as start-up problems in North America were overcome.
"We are over the worst of the difficulties in the start-up in North Carolina and I would expect profits to show steady improvement," he said.
Profits in the power drives sector rose nine percent last year, while the process control and packaging & materials division saw results rise by respectively 10 and one percent.
Profits in specialist engineering rose three percent.
In the building products and polymeric products divisions results were respectively up two and down 12 percent.
Strachan, brought in early in 1996, announced BTR's restructuring programme in September, together with exceptional provisions totalling 462 million stg.
But Strachan said no further such exceptional items would be necessary. "That is highly unlikely," he said.
BTR already sold off businesses representing 1.75 billion pounds of 1995 sales against a 2.3 billion pound target by the end of 1997.
But Strachan said the conglomerate wants to do more than just sell operations.

"We continue to invest in our core businesses with new technology and product development and also our acquisition strategy is focused on our major business groups," Strachan said. "We are finding attractive opportunities in emerging markets," he added. -- London Newsroom +44 171 542 7717
